entries.name: Backgammon is played by two persons

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 271

entries.evidence: Backgammon is played by two persons, on a special "board" with thirty "men," fifteen white and fifteen black (or red), similar to those used for the game of Draughts.

tests.mutation: Players.Adversary returned the player himself (`player` for `player == Player.White ? Player.Black : Player.White`), so one person plays alone; this test went red. It went red too with Players.Both reduced to White alone, and with a third value, Red, added to Player.

entries.note: men-count took the thirty men from this sentence and left the two persons in it. The engine's Player type and every player-relative rule rest on the count; nothing mapped it.

entries.name: Thirty men, fifteen to a side

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 271

entries.evidence: Backgammon is played by two persons, on a special "board" with thirty "men," fifteen white and fifteen black (or red), similar to those used for the game of Draughts.

tests.mutation: Position.ToSlots refused only a side of more than fifteen (`total > MenPerPlayer` for `total != MenPerPlayer`); this test went red on fourteen.
Position.MenPerPlayer set to 14; this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate both figures: thirty men, and fifteen to a side. player-count maps the two persons in the same sentence; the two entries quote one span and are accountable to different halves of it, which is the speed-limit / speed-within-limit split applied to a sentence rather than a paragraph.

entries.name: The board is two tables, inner and outer

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: The board is so placed in use that the two compartments, known as "tables," shall lie longitudinally between the players. One of these is known as the "outer," the other as the "inner" or "home" table. Which of the two is for the time being the inner and which the outer table is governed by the arrangement of the men at starting. With the men placed as in Fig. 1, the right hand is the inner or home table, and the left hand consequently the outer table. The portions of the two latter nearest to each player are known as _his_ inner and outer tables respectively.

tests.mutation: Geometry.QuarterOf ended the inner table at pip 5 (`<= 5 => Quarter.OwnInner`); this test went red.
The same mutation, the inner table ending at pip 5; this test went red.

entries.note: Player-relative structure only: two compartments, one inner and one outer, and the portion of each nearest a player is his -- so each player has his own inner (home) and outer table. The last sentence is what makes "his home table" in bearing-off-eligible and "his (the winner's) home table" in game-value name one player's half; the span stopped before it until issue #42, while this note already claimed "two tables a side". The Fig. 1 sentence between is inner-table-handedness's rule and is quoted only because the span must be contiguous; its pointer is declared here for the same reason. How many points a table has is point-designations', not this entry's. Which physical compartment is which is a separate fact - see inner-table-handedness.

crossReferences.unmapped: Fig. 1 is an illustration, not a passage, so there is no entry to name. The sentence making the pointer is inner-table-handedness's rule, carried here only to keep the span contiguous; that entry records the same pointer.

entries.name: How the twenty-four points are named and numbered

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: Each table is marked with twelve "points," six at either end. They are alternately of black and white, black and red, or other distinctive colours. The two points in the inner table farthest from the dividing partition or "bar" are known as the "ace" points, and those next in order as the two or "deuce" points, followed in succession by the three or "trois" points, the four or "quatre" points, the five or "cinque" points, and finally the "six"[65] points, next the bar. The points in the outer tables are designated in like manner, but starting in this case from the dividing partition. The ace point in the outer table is more commonly known as the "bar" point.

tests.mutation: Geometry.NameOf called an outer table's first point the ace point rather than the bar point; this test went red.

entries.note: The corpus defining its own vocabulary, which is a rule and not a preamble. It is the sole authority for a board having twenty-four points and for the two numbering directions - inner tables from the far end, outer tables from the bar. Without it starting-position, enter-from-bar and every bearing-off entry are uninterpretable. Demonstrate all twenty-four designations, both directions, and the outer ace as the bar point. The sentence about the points' colours is not a rule and is quoted because eliding it would break the span: an ellipsis would leave the checker verifying the eleven words before it.

entries.name: Which physical compartment of the board is the inner table

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 272

entries.evidence: With the men placed as in Fig. 1, the right hand is the inner or home table, and the left hand consequently the outer table.
entries.note: The only fact in this corpus that is genuinely beyond a plain-text adapter. The rule is fully determined - but only in Fig. 1, which fixes the left/right orientation the sentence refers to. No engine that models positions player-relatively ever asks; it is recorded because the limit is real, not because it is load-bearing.

crossReferences.unmapped: Fig. 1 is an illustration, not a passage, so there is no entry to name. That the rule is stated only there is this entry's beyondAdapter, which is the record of the same fact from the reader's side.

entries.name: The starting arrangement of the men

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / The Board and Men / p. 273

entries.evidence: The men are arranged at starting as shown in {273} Fig. 1--viz., two of White's men are placed on the ace point in Black's inner table, five are placed on the six point in Black's outer table, three on the deuce point in White's outer table, and five on the six point in White's inner table. Black's men are placed in like manner on the points immediately facing these.

tests.mutation: Setup.Arrangement put the three men on pip 7 instead of pip 8; this test went red.

entries.note: Stated in prose and over-determined. The pips follow from the designations in point-designations: 24(2)/13(5)/8(3)/6(5), fifteen men, mirrored by pip + (25 - pip). Footnote 67 requires exactly three men on the outer deuce point for its blot to exist, and nineteen opening lines in Hints for Play are consistent with this arrangement and no other. Previously mapped beyondAdapter/declined against Fig. 1; that was a misreading of a sentence one paragraph earlier, which is about board handedness. Depends on player-count and men-count: the arrangement places fifteen men for each of the two players (blind mapping).

crossReferences.unmapped: Fig. 1 is an illustration, not a passage. The arrangement it shows is stated in full in the prose after 'viz.', which is what this entry maps.

entries.name: Deciding who begins

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: The game is commenced by each player throwing on the centre of the board a single die, the higher throw of the two giving the right to begin. In the event of a tie, the players throw again.

tests.mutation: Opening.RollForTheRight gave the right to begin to the lower die; this test went red.
The same mutation, the lower die begins; this test went red.
Opening.RollForTheRight accepted the first pair thrown, ties included (`attempt.First > 0` for `attempt.First != attempt.Second`); this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate the higher single die beginning, a tie throwing again, and repeated ties. The single die belongs to this entry and to no other: there is no one-die throw anywhere in a game.

entries.name: The opening thrower may keep the throw or throw again

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: The thrower of the higher number may either adopt the points shown by the two dice as his own throw, or throw again.

tests.mutation: Opening.OpeningThrow inverted the option (`!adopt ? roll.Deciding : Throw(source)`); this test went red.
The same mutation, the option inverted; this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate both elections. The adopted throw can never be doublets, because a tie throws again and the two dice therefore differ - a consequence of opening-roll that is invisible from either entry alone, and that wires an adopt branch into the doublets path if it is missed. Depends on throw-two-dice ('or throw again' is a throw with both dice); enabled by opening-roll, which alone produces 'the thrower of the higher number' (blind mapping).

entries.name: The thrower calls his throw, the higher number first

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: After throwing, he calls the number of the throw, the higher number first, as "six deuce," "cinque trois," "quatre ace," or as the case may be, and then proceeds to make his move in accordance with it.
entries.note: Read and declined, not absent (docs/decisions/0009): the corpus states the procedure and it is normative, not advice. Out because it is table protocol an engine has no part in: the call is spoken by one player to the other, it moves no man and changes no position, and the corpus attaches nothing to it -- no consequence of a miscall, and the move is made "in accordance with" the throw, not with the call. An engine is handed the dice and gives the same answer to every question whether or not anyone called them. The order of naming, higher first, is the convention the corpus's own throw names follow ("six trois", and the headings die-faces quotes), and naming is not a rule the engine applies. It had no entry until the blind mapping trial flagged it (issue #42), which was the state 0009 exists to remove: a stated rule with no verdict.

entries.name: All subsequent throws use both dice

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: All subsequent throws are with both dice.

tests.mutation: Opening.Throw threw one die and doubled its face instead of throwing the pair; this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate that every throw after the opening roll is two dice. The evidence previously read "the opening throw is one die and every later throw two", which is a paraphrase of opening-roll's sentence rather than of this one; the single die is that entry's and nothing in the corpus attaches a move to it (finding 10 of the engine's MAP-FINDINGS.md, confirmed as imprecise rather than wrong). Suspended by full-table-suspension (docs/decisions/0011): a wholly suspended player does not throw -- 'the adversary continuing to throw and move' -- so this rule is unreachable on his turn, and an engine that throws for him anyway consumes the generator and changes every later throw.

entries.name: Each die moves one man that many points

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: The number uppermost on each die entitles the player to move one man forward a corresponding number of points. Thus if he threw "six trois," he is entitled to move one man six points onward, and then the same or another man {274} three points onward.

tests.mutation: Movement.MovesForDie let only the rearmost man move, so the trois could not go to another man; this test went red.
Movement.MovesForDie offered a move past the ace point before bearing off (`to < 1 || IsPermittedDestination(...)` for `to >= 1 && IsPermittedDestination(...)`); this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate a throw played on one man and on two, and the worked "six trois" example. The span straddles the page break and carries the {274} marker verbatim; the rule sentence is on p. 273 and the citation follows it. Suspended by three rules (docs/decisions/0011): enter-from-bar while a man is up, full-table-suspension while the player's play is altogether suspended, and bearing-off-eligible once every man is home, from which point bearing-off-move-or-remove governs every forward move and a number unusable forward bears a man off instead of being lost. Depends on direction-of-travel: "move one man forward" is a distance and a direction, and this sentence states only the distance (issue #42).

entries.name: The twenty-four points are one course with two ends

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 273

entries.evidence: The movement of the men of each player is from the ace point in his opponent's home table towards the like point in his own

tests.mutation: Geometry.Mirror returned its argument, so both players' courses ran the same way; this test went red.
The same mutation, Mirror as the identity; this test went red.

entries.note: move-by-pip gives distance only. This is the sole authority for direction, and for the two players travelling opposite ways over the same twenty-four points - which is what makes a pip count, a blot and bearing off mean anything. Depends on board-tables, where a player's own home table ('his own') is stated (blind mapping).

entries.name: Doublets are played twice over

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: In the event of his throwing the same points with both dice (known as "doublets"), he is entitled to play the throw twice over. Suppose, for example, that he throws two aces; he may move one or more men forward to an aggregate extent of four points. If he throw double deuces, he may move to an aggregate extent of eight points; if double threes, twelve points, and so on.

tests.mutation: Movement.Entitlement gave doublets two numbers instead of four; this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate all three worked examples: aces to four points, deuces to eight, threes to twelve. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked; the {274} marker falls two sentences earlier. Suspended by full-table-suspension as well as enter-from-bar (docs/decisions/0011): a suspended player throws no doublets to play.

entries.name: A man may be played only to a permitted point

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: The right to move is subject to a certain qualification--viz., that a man can only be played to a point which is either vacant or occupied by one or more men of the player, or by one man only of the adversary.

tests.mutation: Movement.IsPermittedDestination refused a point holding one adversary man (`== 0` for `<= 1`); this test went red.

ambiguity.question: Three sentences later the corpus states the destinations open to a man entering from the bar as 'a vacant point or blot', omitting this rule's second arm -- a point the player's own men hold. Either this general qualification on 'the right to move' governs entry as well and the entry sentence is shorthand for it, or entry is a stated exception to it. Each reading is internally coherent and the corpus chooses neither.

entries.note: Decided: the general rule governs entry. The reading is observable in exactly one test -- EnterFromBarTests.Entry_is_permitted_on_a_point_the_entering_players_own_men_hold -- which fails under the other one. Demonstrate vacant, own men, exactly one adversary man, and two or more refused; and entry from the bar onto a point the entering player's own men hold, which is where this rule and enter-from-bar disagree. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked. Suspended by full-table-suspension (docs/decisions/0011): the qualification applies to the right to move, and a player whose play is altogether suspended has none. It is not suspended by enter-from-bar, because under docs/decisions/0006 this rule governs the entering man's destination too.

entries.name: Two men make a point

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: A player getting two men on a given point is said to "make" such point, and as he thereby secures such men from capture, and at the same time impedes the onward march of the enemy

tests.mutation: Position.HasMadePoint required three men (`>= 3` for `>= 2`); this test went red.

The same mutation, three men to a point; this test went red. Before it was strengthened it checked only the six point, which starts with five men, and stayed green; it now checks White's 24, which starts with exactly two.

entries.note: Demonstrate two men and one. The span stops before the sentence's last clause, "it is always an object to do this", which is advice inside a normative section and is dropped rather than mapped - the instance docs/method.md names. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked.

entries.name: A single man is a blot and may be hit

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: A single man on a given point is known as a "blot," and not only does not prevent the enemy playing to that point, but in the event of its being "hit"--_i.e._, reached by an adverse throw, it is "taken up" (placed on the bar between the two tables), and, however far advanced it may have been, has to begin its journey anew from the inner table of the adversary.

tests.mutation: Position.Apply removed a hit blot from its point without putting it on the bar; this test went red.
The same mutation, a hit blot not put on the bar; this test went red.

entries.note: Demonstrate that a blot hit goes to the bar and restarts from the adversary's inner table, however far advanced. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked. Suspended by full-table-suspension (docs/decisions/0011) on the suspended player's own turn: a hit is made by a move, and he makes none. His blots are still hit by the adversary, whose turn this gate does not reach.

entries.name: A man on the bar re-enters before any other man moves

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: Nor can such man again start on its journey until its owner is fortunate enough to make a throw corresponding with a vacant point or blot in such table. Until he does this, the play of his other men is suspended.

tests.mutation: Movement.MovesForDie never took the entry branch, so a player with a man up moved his other men; this test went red.
The same mutation, the entry branch never taken; this test went red.
Movement.MustEnterFromBar held only for exactly one man up (`== 1` for `> 0`); this test went red.
The same mutation, exactly one man up; this test went red.
Movement.MovesForDie refused entry onto a point the entering player's own men hold -- the strict reading 0006 rejected; this test went red.

ambiguity.question: This sentence names two destinations for an entering man, 'a vacant point or blot', where legal-destination three sentences earlier names three -- it omits a point the entering player's own men hold. Either the general qualification governs entry and this is shorthand for it, or entry is narrower than ordinary movement. Read strictly, this sentence and full-table-suspension are exact negations of one another, which is what makes both readings coherent.

entries.note: Decided: the general rule governs entry, so a point the entering player's own men hold is open to him. The reading is observable in EnterFromBarTests.Entry_is_permitted_on_a_point_the_entering_players_own_men_hold, which fails under the other one. Demonstrate entry available and unavailable, all other men suspended while one is up, and entry onto a point the entering player's own men hold. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked. Suspended by full-table-suspension (docs/decisions/0011): a completely full table leaves no throw 'corresponding with a vacant point or blot', and the corpus does not have the player throw to find that out -- his play is altogether suspended. Depends on legal-destination because the decision makes that rule the entering man's destination test, so this entry cannot be built as decided without it; blot-hit reaching it first is ordering by accident, not the reason. Depends on point-designations: "a throw corresponding with a vacant point" names the point in the adversary's inner table that each number enters on, and the numbering is stated only there (both issue #42). Depends on direction-of-travel: the man begins 'its journey anew' and the entering point is counted along that journey. Enabled by blot-hit, the only rule that puts a man on the bar (both from the blind mapping).

entries.name: Play is wholly suspended against a full home table

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 274

entries.evidence: If the adverse player's home table is completely full--_i.e._, each point occupied by two or more men, his play is altogether suspended, the adversary continuing to throw and move until the course of play again throws open one or more points in his table.

tests.mutation: Movement.IsWhollySuspended always returned false; this test went red.
Movement.IsWhollySuspended counted a point as full on two men of either side -- the literal reading 0006 rejected; this test went red.

ambiguity.question: 'Completely full -- i.e., each point occupied by two or more men' is unqualified, so two of the entering player's own men satisfy it. Either 'full' means full of the adverse player's men, which is the only reading consistent with the general rule governing entry, or it means occupied by anyone, which is the exact negation of enter-from-bar's 'a vacant point or blot'. The corpus determines both readings and chooses neither.

entries.note: Decided: 'full' means adversely full. The reading is observable in FullTableSuspensionTests.A_point_held_by_the_entering_players_own_men_does_not_make_the_table_full, which fails under the other one. The same decision settles whether both players can be suspended at once through play: under this reading they cannot, so the engine's UnsupportedInteraction for that position answers only what a caller may assert. Demonstrate six points held by two or more, the adversary throwing and moving alone, and six points all occupied but one of them by the entering player's own men, which suspends nobody. Depends on made-point, which is what "each point occupied by two or more men" means. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked. It suspends seven entries, each named in that entry's suspendedBy with the judgement in its note (docs/decisions/0011). Enabled by blot-hit: 'his play' is the play of the owner of the man taken up, the subject of the two sentences before, so the suspension is reachable only once a man is on the bar (blind mapping).

entries.name: The whole throw must be played if it can be

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Playing / p. 275

entries.evidence: Any part of a throw which cannot be played is lost to the thrower, but every player is compelled to play the whole of his throw if it is possible to do so.

tests.mutation: LegalPlays.For offered every partial play as well as the whole one (a terminal at every node, and no filter to the compelled use); this test went red. The maximal filter alone removed was not caught by it, because from the start every leaf is whole.
The same mutation, partial plays offered; this test went red. Re-observed after the fixture's thirteen other men moved from off the board to White's ace point (map 3.0.0, rows 12 and 13); still red.

LegalPlays.For declined only when more than two uses were maximal (`> 2` for `> 1`), silently playing the first; this test went red. Re-observed after the fixture's thirteen other men moved from off the board to White's ace point (map 3.0.0, blind-mapping resolution rows 12 and 13); still red.

The same mutation, the incomparable case resolved silently; this test went red. Re-observed after bearing-off-eligible's declines were excluded from the comparison (map 3.0.0, rows 12 and 13); still red.

LegalPlays.For compelled only the higher number where the throw could not be played whole: when the one playable number was the lower, it returned the empty play instead; this test went red (the trois case). Before it was strengthened it tested only a playable six and stayed green. It also went red when any throw not playable whole was forfeited entirely. Removing the maximal-use filter cannot turn it red, and no test of this case could: where only one die is ever playable every unextendable line uses that die once, so the filter removes nothing. Re-observed (the trois case) after the fixture's thirteen other men moved from off the board to White's ace point (map 3.0.0, rows 12 and 13); still red.

LegalPlays.For exempted a player with a man up from the compulsion -- every line, partial ones included, offered with no maximal filter -- which is the enter-from-bar suspension map 3.0.0 removed (blind-mapping resolution row 66); this test went red, and so did EnterFromBarTests.The_second_man_up_is_still_up_when_the_first_has_entered. It went red too under the partial-plays mutation above.

ambiguity.question: An unplayable part is lost and the whole must be played 'if it is possible'. The text does not say what happens when either die alone is playable but not both -- a case every modern ruleset settles explicitly.

entries.note: status and ambiguity.fate are independent (docs/decisions/0005), so an engine may implement this rule and still decline the case the question names -- which is the whole of what it declines. Read as an obligation to play a set of numbers that cannot be extended, the compulsion settles every other throw from the text: doublets are never ambiguous, and a throw with one playable die compels it. Demonstrate a throw fully playable, partly playable, and unplayable. Where the entry is implemented the conformance verdict covers every case but the one named, and the declining case ships WholeThrowTests.Where_either_die_alone_can_be_played_but_not_both_the_corpus_does_not_settle_it. Cited p. 273 until the span was quoted and checked; the sentence is on p. 275, two pages on. Suspended by full-table-suspension (docs/decisions/0011): with no throw there is no whole of a throw to compel. Not suspended by enter-from-bar: a man up suspends 'the play of his other men', not the throw, and 'every player' must still play the whole throw where he can, entering first (corrected in the blind mapping). Depends on doublets: the whole of a doublet throw is four parts.

entries.name: Bearing off begins when all men are home

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 275

entries.evidence: When either player has succeeded in getting all his men into his home table, he proceeds to "bear them off"--_i.e._, to remove them from the board.

tests.mutation: BearingOff.IsEligible ignored a man on pip 7 (the outer-table loop started at 8); this test went red.

LegalPlays.For never tested BearingOff.HasReEnteredMidBearOff, so the throw was played as though the man had to come home again (the reading map 3.0.0 leaves unresolved, blind-mapping resolution rows 12 and 13); this test went red. Replaces A_man_hit_back_out_mid_bear_off_stops_it, whose IsEligible assertion was a reading of that question and whose suspension assertion moved to BearingOffSuspensionTests.

BearingOff.HasReEnteredMidBearOff held without a man borne off (the `BorneOff(player) == 0` arm dropped), so a player not yet home at all declined; this test went red. It went red too with the man-at-home arm dropped (`return outside;` for `return home && outside;`).

ambiguity.question: The stage begins 'when either player has succeeded in getting all his men into his home table', and the chapter never says whether it lasts. If one of his men is hit after he has begun to bear off and then re-enters, the text does not say whether he may go on bearing off the men still at home or must first bring every man home again.

entries.note: Demonstrate all fifteen home and fourteen home. A man hit back out mid-bear-off is the case the question names; it was a demonstration here, with no reading recorded, until the blind mapping. Depends on board-tables: the rule is written in "his home table", and which half of the board is a player's own home table is stated there and nowhere else (issue #42).

entries.name: Each throw may move within the table or remove a man

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 275

entries.evidence: When the game has reached this stage, each throw entitles the player either to move forward a man or men (to the extent indicated by the throw) within the limits of his own table, or to remove men from the corresponding points.

tests.mutation: BearingOff.MovesForDie never removed a man from the point the die names; this test went red.
BearingOff.MovesForDie offered no forward move within the table; this test went red.

Movement.MovesForDie tested bearing off before the bar, BearingOff.IsEligible ignored the bar and BearingOff.MovesForDie dropped its enter-from-bar refusal, so a player bearing off with a man up bore off instead of entering; this test went red. The suspension is map 3.0.0's (blind-mapping resolution rows 11, 14 and 17).

entries.note: Demonstrate the worked distribution that follows this sentence, for both the quatre and the trois. The span is the sentence that states the rule; the worked example runs on across the {276} marker and is the demonstration, not the statement. Depends on move-by-pip: "to move forward a man or men (to the extent indicated by the throw)" is move-by-pip's forward move, one man per number, restated for this phase rather than redefined -- move-by-pip is suspended here and this rule reuses what it states (issue #42). Depends on legal-destination: a forward move inside the home table is still refused by a made point and still takes up a blot. Suspended by enter-from-bar (blind mapping, examples/hoyle-backgammon/blind-mapping/): a man up suspends 'the play of his other men', bearing off included. Depends on point-designations: 'the corresponding points' are named by the number thrown.

entries.name: An unusable number bears off from the highest occupied point

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 276

entries.evidence: If, however, he throws a number which he cannot deal with after either of these fashions--_e.g._, a six, he is entitled to bear off a man from his highest occupied point, in this case the cinque.

tests.mutation: BearingOff.MovesForDie applied the modern rule, bearing off only from a point below the die; this test went red and no other did.
BearingOff.MovesForDie bore off from the lowest occupied point instead of the highest; this test went red.

Movement.MovesForDie tested bearing off before the bar, BearingOff.IsEligible ignored the bar and BearingOff.MovesForDie dropped its enter-from-bar refusal, so a player bearing off with a man up bore off instead of entering; this test went red. The suspension is map 3.0.0's (blind-mapping resolution rows 11, 14 and 17).

entries.note: Clear, correct, and the opposite of what a modern player expects: a number that neither of the two fashions can deal with bears a man off the highest occupied point even where men still stand above it, which a modern ruleset refuses. Under docs/decisions/0005 the entry names the test that fails under the assumed reading: BearingOffDetailTests.A_blocked_forward_move_bears_off_from_the_highest_point_men_still_above_it. It is the one case in the suite where Hoyle's rule and the modern rule differ. Demonstrate the six-throw example, and a usable throw, which must be played forward instead. Cited p. 275 until the span was quoted and checked. Suspended by enter-from-bar (blind mapping, examples/hoyle-backgammon/blind-mapping/): a man up suspends 'the play of his other men', bearing off included.

entries.name: Doublets bear off or move, or both

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 276

entries.name: A win is a hit, a gammon, or a backgammon

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Bearing off the Men / p. 276

entries.evidence: If the adversary has got all his men into his own home table, and has begun to bear off, the game of the winner is known as a "hit." If the winner has borne off all his men before his adversary has begun to do the same, the game is known as a "gammon." The loser is said to be "gammoned," and pays double the agreed stake. If the winner has borne off all his men while the adversary has still a man or men "up" (_i.e._, on the bar) or in his (the winner's) home table, the game is a "backgammon," and the loser pays {277} either thrice or four times (as may have been agreed) the amount of the single stake.

tests.mutation: Outcome.ValueOf called it a gammon while the loser had borne off two or fewer (`<= 2` for `== 0`); this test went red.

Outcome.ValueOf ignored a loser's man on the bar; this test went red. Re-observed after the loser was given two men borne off, so that he is not also a gammon (map 3.0.0, blind-mapping resolution row 52); under the mutation he now declines as the uncovered finish, and the test still went red.
Outcome.ValueOf called the uncovered finish a hit instead of declining; this test went red.
Outcome.ValueOf dropped the overlap decline and tested backgammon first, as it did before map 3.0.0 named the overlap in game-value's question (blind-mapping resolution row 52); this test went red.

ambiguity.question: The three named results do not cover every finish. Written as predicates on the loser they are: all his men home and he has begun to bear off (a hit); he has not begun to bear off (a gammon); he has a man up or in the winner's home table (a backgammon). A loser who has borne off a man, been taken up, re-entered and run that man clear of the winner's home table answers none of them, and the corpus does not say what such a win is worth. Nor are they disjoint: a loser who has borne off nothing and has a man up answers both 'before his adversary has begun to do the same' (a gammon) and 'a man or men "up"' (a backgammon), and the corpus does not say which result he suffers.

entries.note: Was recorded clarity: clear, which asserts the corpus determines one answer for every valid input, while the engine returned RequiresInterpretation citing this entry -- the live violation of the correspondence table. The gap case is reachable and not a curiosity: the winner hits a bearing-off opponent's blot from outside, which he can only do while still running, and then finishes first. Demonstrate all three results -- adversary bearing off; not yet bearing off; a man up or in the winner's home table -- and the finish none of the three names; the declining case ships GameValueTests.The_three_named_results_do_not_cover_every_finish. The overlap between the gammon and backgammon conditions has been part of the question since the blind mapping; before it, an ordering (backgammon first) had been chosen and recorded nowhere. entries.name: The faces a die bears, and the throws a pair of them can show

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Hints for Play / p. 277

entries.evidence: We will go _seriatim_ through all the possible throws. In some instances alternative methods will be given, according as the player aims merely at securing a hit, and is content, therefore, to play for safety, or elects to {278} play a more risky game upon the chance of securing a gammon. This case often arises where the player has already lost the first hit of a rubber, in which case, if he loses the next game, he has lost the rubber also; but if he can secure a gammon (reckoning as a double game), he becomes the winner of the rubber. ACES.--(The best possible throw at starting.) Play two men on your "bar" point, and two on your cinque point.[67] DEUCE ACE.--For a hit, play the deuce from the five men in your adversary's outer-table, and the ace from the ace point in his inner table. For a gammon, play the ace from the six to the ace point in your own table. DEUCES.--For a hit, play two from the six to the quatre point in your own table, and the other two from the ace to the trois point in your opponent's inner table. For a gammon, play the second pair from the five men in his outer table. TROIS ACE.--Make your cinque point. TROIS DEUCE.--The approved play is to carry two men from the five in your adversary's outer table to the quatre and cinque points in your own outer table. This, of course, makes two blots. To avoid this, some, for a hit, play one man from the same {279} point to the _deuce_ point in the above-mentioned table, but the bolder play is to be preferred. DOUBLE TROIS.--There are three ways of playing this throw. Some players make the bar point. The more usual play is, for a hit, to play two to the cinque point in the player's own, and the other two to the quatre point in the adversary's table. For a gammon, play the last two from the six to the trois point in your own table. QUATRE ACE.--Play the quatre from the five men in your opponent's outer table, and the ace from his ace point. (Timid players, fearing to leave two blots, sometimes play the whole throw from the first-mentioned point, but the plan is not to be recommended.) QUATRE DEUCE.--Make your quatre point. QUATRE TROIS.--Play two men from the five in your adversary's outer table. DOUBLE QUATRE.--Play two men from the ace to the cinque point in the adversary's inner table, and two from the five in his outer table. For a gammon, play two men only, from the point last mentioned to the cinque point in your own table. CINQUE ACE.--Play the cinque from the five men in your adversary's outer table, and the ace from the ace point in his inner table. For a gammon, play the ace from the six to the cinque point in your own table. CINQUE DEUCE.--Play both men from the five in your adversary's outer table. CINQUE TROIS.--Make your trois point. CINQUE QUATRE.--Move one man from your adversary's ace point to the trois point in his outer table. {280} DOUBLE CINQUE.--Carry two men from the five in the adversary's outer table, and make your trois point. SIX ACE.--Make your bar point. SIX DEUCE.--Move a man from the five in your adversary's outer table to the cinque point in your own table. SIX TROIS, SIX QUATRE, SIX CINQUE.--Carry one man from your adversary's ace point as far as the throw will permit. SIXES.--Place two men on your adversary's bar point, and two on your own.

tests.mutation: Die.D6 constructed a five-faced die; this test went red.

entries.note: The only authority in this corpus for a die having six faces, and the engine's DicePair.OfSixes had none before this entry existed (issue #20). The corpus never writes "six" of a die. It declares the enumeration exhaustive -- "all the possible throws" -- and then names twenty-one: ACES, DEUCE ACE, DEUCES, TROIS ACE, TROIS DEUCE, DOUBLE TROIS, QUATRE ACE, QUATRE DEUCE, QUATRE TROIS, DOUBLE QUATRE, CINQUE ACE, CINQUE DEUCE, CINQUE TROIS, CINQUE QUATRE, DOUBLE CINQUE, SIX ACE, SIX DEUCE, SIX TROIS, SIX QUATRE, SIX CINQUE, SIXES. (Nineteen headings; SIX TROIS, SIX QUATRE and SIX CINQUE share one.) An unordered pair over n faces has n(n+1)/2 throws, and n(n+1)/2 = 21 has exactly one positive solution, n = 6. Demonstrate all twenty-one throws and the six faces, and that no seventh face is admitted. Why an entry in a section another entry declines: strategy-advice declines the advice, not the section. scope is decided per rule (docs/decisions/0009); a section is a unit of layout and has no scope of its own, which is why the corpus's only statement of the throw space sat unmapped inside a section everyone read as excluded. The span is long because the rule is stated by extension: the exhaustiveness claim and the twenty-first throw are 601 words apart, no ellipsis is permitted, and the whole-table rule requires the whole enumeration and never a sample. The advice interleaved through it is strategy-advice's subject and is carried because eliding it would break the match. Limit stated where the claim is: the corpus states the throw space and never says the dice are fair, so nothing here licenses a distribution -- only the support.

entries.note: The corpus does not contain this rule, which is a different verdict from declining to cover one, and `absentFrom` is what separates them (docs/decisions/0009). The cited sentence is where the rule would be if the corpus had it: the doubling cube is a piece of apparatus, and this sentence enumerates the apparatus and closes the list ("complete the apparatus of the game"). The stakes passage on pp. 276-277 closes a second list -- "the value of the game depends upon the stage reached by the adverse player, as follows", then three results and nothing else -- so a stake that could be raised during play has no room there either. Four terms are searched for and none occurs in pages 271-280; check-locators.py fails this entry if one turns up. Stated where the claim is: absence of those four terms is not absence of the rule. The corpus could state it in words nobody searched for, and no check reaches that. Note also that the search is bounded by the declared extent and must be: "doubling" does not occur in the backgammon chapter and does occur elsewhere in the same volume. Previously cited "(absent)", which is what issue #29 was filed about.

entries.name: The advisory principles of play

locator.citation: BACKGAMMON / Hints for Play / p. 277

entries.evidence: A leading principle is to "make points" whenever you fairly can, especially in or close to your home table.
entries.note: Non-normative. Advice, not rules -- but similar advice appears inside the normative sections too ('it is always an object to do this'). Nothing is demanded of the engine. The span is the opening sentence of the advice being declined, quoted so that the citation is checkable: an out-of-scope verdict is a verdict about a passage, and a passage that cannot be located is a verdict about nothing. **This verdict is about the advice and not about the section that holds it.** Hints for Play also states die-faces, which is scope: in and load-bearing, and reading this entry as excluding the section is what cost the map the number of faces on a die (issue #20, docs/decisions/0009). A section is a unit of the corpus's layout; scope is a judgement about a rule.
